extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals, journalists, and general readers seeking guidance on press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the purpose, standard structure, length, distribution methods, and etiquette for preparing and issuing press releases for journalists and media outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release (also known as a media release) is an official statement delivered to members of the news media for the purpose of providing new information, creating an official statement, or making an announcement directed for public release. Press releases are also considered a primary source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically delivered electronically and often prepared 'ready to use' so outlets can publish quickly; may be subject to a news embargo. Be aware that as primary-source material issued by an interested party, press releases can be favorable toward the issuing organization and frame a topic according to its preferred criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letterhead or logo
rubrics_metrics.description: Include letterhead or a logo at the top of the press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard professional format used by public relations professionals; helps identify the issuing organization immediately to journalists and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide media contact information — name, phone number, email address, mailing address, or other contact information for the PR or other media relations contact person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential so journalists can follow up for clarification, additional quotes, or interviews. Omit or obscure contacts if intentionally anonymous, but this reduces credibility and follow-up potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline
rubrics_metrics.description: A headline used to grab the attention of journalists and briefly summarize the news in one to six words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep it concise and newsworthy; the headline should immediately communicate the core news so busy editors can assess relevance at a glance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dek (sub-headline)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dek is a sub-headline that describes the headline in more detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the dek to add a short clarifying detail or hook that doesn't fit in the headline but helps editors decide whether to read further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline
rubrics_metrics.description: A dateline contains the release date and usually the originating city of the press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the date listed is after the date the information was actually sent to the media, the sender is typically requesting a news embargo; dateline placement and dating communicates timing and origin to journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction (lead) — answer the Five Ws
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction is the first paragraph in a press release and generally gives basic answers to the questions of who, what, when, where and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow journalism principles (Five Ws, inverted pyramid) so the lead provides the essential facts up front; avoid burying the core information deep in the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body — supporting detail
rubrics_metrics.description: The body provides further explanation, statistics, background, or other details relevant to the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subsequent paragraphs to expand on the lead with credible facts, quotes, context, and supporting data. Ensure facts are checkable and distinguish clearly between factual claims and promotional language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate
rubrics_metrics.description: A boilerplate is generally a short 'about' section, providing independent background on the issuing company, organization, or individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep it concise and factual so journalists can use it as a neutral organizational description; avoid hyperbolic marketing copy in the boilerplate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close (end marker)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally the symbol '-30-' or '###' (or the word 'ends' in some countries) appears after the boilerplate or body and before the media contact information, indicating to media that the release has ended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a conventional end marker so editors know the release copy is complete; inconsistent or missing end markers can cause confusion in copy-and-paste workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and paragraph count
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release body generally consists of four to five paragraphs with a word limit ranging from 400 to 500, though length can vary from about 300 to 800 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep releases concise and focused; longer releases may be appropriate for complex announcements but risk being ignored by time-pressed journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution model — newswire vs self-distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional distribution hires a publicity agency to write and distribute via newswires; an alternative is self-distributed press releases, sent directly to media or via paid/free distribution services that provide contact lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose distribution based on audience, budget, and control needs. Newswires can broaden reach and lend formality; self-distribution is common for SMEs, political institutions, governments, and courts, and may be more targeted but requires better contact-list management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video news release (VNR) considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Video news releases are pre-taped video programs or clips that can be aired intact by TV stations; they may include staged interviews and can be produced at high cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that some broadcast outlets discourage VNRs due to potential negative public perception and credibility concerns. VNRs can be repurposed (podcasts, web) and extended via community websites, but transparency about production/context is important to maintain trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargo handling and etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: If a press release (draft or final) is distributed before public release it is typically subject to an embargo requesting news organizations not report the story until a specified date or time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An embargo is not legally binding unless the journalist signs an NDA; violating an embargo risks damaging relationships and reputations. Publicists are encouraged to share embargoed information only with journalists they trust and who are willing to honor the embargo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pros and limitations for journalists (use with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using press releases can save news outlets time and improve output because material is pre-packaged; however, releases constrain format and style and can be favorable to the issuing organization, framing topics to its advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should treat press releases as primary-source material requiring verification and awareness of bias; reliance on press releases can reduce time for independent reporting and fact-checking and contribute to 'churnalism.'
